asDecan.p: Every sign is split into three slices of ten degrees, called decans, and each slice has a planet and a small card of its own. Your Sun sits in the first ten degrees of Pisces, and in the Golden Dawn order that slice belongs to Saturn. Saturn has no special standing in Pisces. It isn't at home there and it isn't weakened either. It's more of a guest, and like most guests it picks up the manners of the house, which here is Jupiter's (Neptune's, if you use the modern ruler). Pisces is mutable water, feeling that moves and changes shape, and Saturn is the planet of limits, time and the sensible decision nobody wants to make. A sober visitor in that sign gives you the Eight of Cups, someone who feels all of it and still gets up and goes. The next slice is Jupiter's Nine of Cups, which is far happier to stay put, and then Mars and the Ten. The Moon is your Sun card, the whole of Pisces, and this is its first and most serious stretch.

You're usually the first to notice when something has gone flat. A dinner party is going well, the food's good, everyone's laughing, and somewhere around dessert you realise you'd quite like to be at home, and you couldn't say why. A group chat you used to love starts to feel like homework, so you mute it, and six months later you've drifted out of it without a single argument. You can stay in a job for years past its use-by date, because leaving without a proper reason feels irresponsible to the Saturn part of you, and then one Monday you hand in your notice and everyone's shocked except you. On a Sunday with nothing planned you might clear out a wardrobe, get oddly teary over a jumper from ten years ago, and put it in the charity bag anyway.

The less obvious gift is that you can put a dream on a timetable. Plenty of Pisces people carry a lovely idea for a book, a garden, a retreat, a second career in music therapy, and it stays an idea for twenty years. With Saturn running your slice you're the one who gets up at six and writes for an hour before work, every weekday, for two years, and then actually sends the thing off. You also leave well, which is rarer than people think. When you finish a job you train your replacement properly and write the handover notes nobody else would bother with. When a friendship has run its course you tend to say so kindly, in person, so nobody's left guessing for months. Quite a few of your exes still send you a birthday message.

The harder thing to see in yourself is that leaving can turn into your answer for everything. A friendship hits a rough patch and you just start replying a bit later each time. Work gets dull for a month and you're on job sites by Thursday. Because you do it quietly and politely, nobody gets a chance to argue with you, and to be honest that's partly why you do it that way. Have a look at the card. The figure has their back turned and the cups behind them are still standing, all eight, in perfectly good order. Sometimes what you walked away from only needed one awkward conversation or a bit of repair. The people left behind often say the same thing afterwards, that they had no idea anything was wrong, and they're usually telling the truth.

Under real strain, a bereavement, a redundancy, months of being overlooked at work, the first thing you tend to do is go small and get organised. You tidy, you make lists, you cancel plans with a polite text, and you get very good at sounding fine on the phone. Saturn likes a routine when things fall apart. About a week in, the Pisces side comes up through the floor, often at an odd moment, crying in the supermarket car park or lying awake at three going over everything you might have done differently. The people close to you can feel shut out during the organised stage and then frightened by how low you get in the second one. What helps is someone checking in on a schedule, the same friend at the same time a few days a week, whether or not you say you're alright. Let them keep it up for a month, even once you're sleeping again.

You don't commit lightly, and once you do you treat it almost like a vow, which is Saturn talking. The part partners don't always understand is that you need to go off on your own now and then to stay in love. After an argument you might put your coat on and walk for an hour, and someone who doesn't know you well yet can read that as you leaving them. You're coming back. You just need some distance to work out what you actually feel. It helps to say that out loud early on, on a calm day, so they don't panic the first time the front door closes. Keeping score in silence is the other habit to watch. You'll give up a lot for someone, weekends, a move interstate, and then years later it all comes out in one sentence during a fight about the bins.

You're good in jobs where something soft needs a firm frame around it. Running the volunteer roster at a hospice, editing other people's poetry, managing the timetable at a music school, pharmacy, case management in social work, conservation in a museum. You can take in a lot of feeling from clients or patients and still get the paperwork in on time, and that combination is less common than it ought to be. The trouble is that you tend to outgrow roles quietly. You do a job well for three or four years, get the promotion, and then a flatness sets in that you can't explain to your manager, because nothing's actually wrong. Before you resign, try changing the job from the inside. Ask for a different project or a different team, or drop a day. Sometimes that's enough, and when it isn't you'll know properly.

At twenty this decan can be quite hard on itself. You feel everything, Saturn tells you you're being too much, and you swing between drifting along and setting yourself very strict rules about how to live. A lot of early Pisces people leave things abruptly in their twenties, a course, a city, a relationship, and don't really understand why until later. By the mid-thirties there's usually been at least one departure you're proud of and one you regret, and that pair teaches you an enormous amount. You get slower to leave and clearer about your reasons when you do. The fifties often bring a settled seriousness about the things you love, music, faith, a craft, a cause, and you tend to give them real hours at last. I've seen a lot of people with this placement do their best work after fifty.

Every few months, sit down with a sheet of paper and list the main things you give your time to: the job, each close friendship, the volunteering, the hobby you keep meaning to drop. Next to each one write a number from one to five for how much it still feeds you. Don't act on it. Keep the sheets in a folder. After a year or so you can see which things have been sliding for a long time and which were only a bad month, and you can decide from that, instead of from one flat Tuesday.
